reviewNotes: Full six-piece physical diagram visually reconstructed with White Kf1, Qa2, Rb1 versus Kh1, Qa8, Rg8. Three mating branches after Kf2+ Kh2 Rh1+, comparing Kxh1, Qxh1 and Qe4 guarding g2. Repeated composition motif is disclosed relative to the earlier digital Pretty Sacrifice; the physical Kf1 root is independently replayed and checked. All six contact sheets reviewed.
transcript: Fools will resign. Wise players might make a draw, but only a true genius would be able to win from this position. You see the two kings are in a standoff, but it is white to move, and it seems like the black king will almost be checkmated once the white king moves. But unfortunately, if we carelessly move the king, actually, this is not a checkmate. The king can move up, and if we try to give another check by moving the king, we are actually going to lose the queen. But at the same time, both the queen [music] and the rook are defended by each other, so there's no progress to be made. But as it turns out, white can win, and we do start by moving the king up one square. Now, of course, black only has one move, to move the king up like this. And this is where we have to start thinking outside the box and come up with an incredible idea to trap the black king. And that idea is the majestic rook to >> [music] >> h1 check, sacrificing the rook completely to the black king. But of course, if the king takes, now we can give a very precise check with our queen, force the king to move back up, and after it does, we are going to give a checkmate like this. But wait a second, black doesn't actually have to capture the sacrificed rook with the king. He can also take it with the black queen. And so now we lost a rook for what? There is no checkmate. But as it turns out, after we use our queen to capture the black rook, this move turns out to be a zugzwang. If the king moves, this is just going to be a checkmate in [music] one move. But at the same time, white is threatening to come down here with his queen, so the black queen has to move somewhere that guard the g2 square. But if it does that, well, actually, now the white queen can come to g1, push the king up and then still deliver a brilliant checkmate. If you like this smart board, read the caption.
